summary.text: The Pax Romana, or 'Roman Peace', was a roughly 200-year golden age of ancient Rome marked by prosperous stability, though revolts and wars still happened.
Traditionally it starts with Augustus's rise in 27 BC and ends in 180 AD with the death of Marcus Aurelius, the last of the Five Good Emperors.
Trade across the Mediterranean grew, the empire reached its greatest size under Trajan in 117, and its population peaked at an estimated 70 million.

facts.label: Population peak
facts.value: Estimated 70 million, 33% of the world's population

facts.label: Peak territory
facts.value: Greatest extent reached under Trajan in 117

facts.label: Gates of Janus
facts.value: Closing them signalled that Rome was at peace

items.prompt: A Roman is asked when the empire counts as being at peace. By Roman thinking, what has to be true?

options.label: No soldier anywhere is fighting a war
Every neighbour has signed a treaty
All opponents have been beaten down and cannot resist
The emperor has refused all new campaigns

items.explain: Romans saw peace not as an absence of war but as a rare situation when all opponents had been beaten down and lost the ability to resist.

items.prompt: A student reads that this era was a golden age of peace, then finds revolts and wars in the same years. How does that fit?

options.label: The golden age label is a modern invention
It was a time of relative peace, with some revolts and wars
The label ignores the wars entirely
Revolts only began once the era ended

items.explain: The period is described as one of relative peace and order that still featured internal revolts and external wars.

items.prompt: Augustus had no good precedent for ruling alone. How did he make a new civil war unlikely?

options.label: He bound the greatest military magnates into one coalition
He disbanded the legions and sent veterans home
He divided the empire among his rival generals
He gave the Senate command of every legion

items.explain: He created a junta of the greatest military magnates with himself as front man, which eliminated the prospect of civil war.

items.prompt: Once the civil wars were over, did calm arrive everywhere at once?

options.label: Yes; every frontier fell quiet immediately
Yes, except for a rebellion in Egypt
No; the civil wars started again within a year
No; fighting went on in Hispania and the Alps

items.explain: The Pax Romana was not immediate despite the end of the civil wars, because fighting continued in Hispania and in the Alps.

items.prompt: Why did incomes across the empire rise in this era?

options.label: Taxes were abolished for all provincial citizens
Mediterranean trade grew and brought large profits
Imports from the East were banned to protect farmers
Free land was handed to every retired soldier

items.explain: Roman trade in the Mediterranean increased, and Romans benefited from large profits, which raised incomes.

items.prompt: Many Romans admired the wealth and honor that a risky war could bring. How did the emperors win them over to peace?

options.label: Through propaganda: coins, ceremonies and literature praising peace
By banning all service in the legions
By paying every citizen a share of spoils
By giving the Senate control of the legions

items.explain: Augustus succeeded through skillful propaganda, and later emperors held lavish ceremonies, issued coins with Pax and patronized literature extolling peace.
